query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, strongly adherent, tin‐enriched anti‐oxidation coating on as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will suppress oxygen ingress and pest oxidation at high temperatures without degrading its room- and elevated-temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting a single-phase, disordered BCC structure with good ductility at room temperature and high yield strength at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin Sn‐modified protective coating (for example by pack cementation or chemical vapor deposition) that, during subsequent exposure, forms a continuous, adherent oxide scale enriched in Sn (or Sn-modified phases) on the alloy’s surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure in air at 800 °C for 5 hours under low mechanical load (or static conditions) to simulate high-temperature service, with subsequent room- and high-temperature tensile evaluations.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, compact oxide layer (influenced by tin) at the alloy surface that minimizes oxygen diffusion into the bulk while remaining adherent to the underlying BCC structure.
generation.mechanism: The tin in the coating promotes the formation of a protective oxide (or modifies scale adhesion) that impedes oxygen penetration (and thus pesting) during high-temperature exposure, while leaving the matrix microstructure and mechanical integrity unaltered.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coated alloy is expected to show a marked reduction in oxygen uptake and pest oxidation at 800 °C (i.e. lower weight gain and improved scale adhesion) while preserving the baseline room- and elevated-temperature tensile strength and ductility observed in the uncoated material.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr suffers from inadequate oxygen resistance (pest oxidation) under high-temperature air exposure despite its useful room- and high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: Temperature: 800 °C; Atmosphere: Air; Exposure duration: ~5 hours; Mechanical loading: near-static condition during exposure; Subsequent mechanical testing at room temperature and around 1000 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum coating thickness, precise tin concentration, and its exact influence on long-term scale stability remain to be established; potential effects on fatigue or creep behavior under cyclic thermal/mechanical loading are also not yet determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr specimens: one group will be coated with the optimized tin-enriched anti-oxidation coating and the other group will remain uncoated. Expose both groups to air at 800 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, use microscopy (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to assess oxide scale continuity and composition, and measure the weight gain due to oxidation. Then perform tensile tests at room temperature and at high temperature (near 1000 °C) to compare mechanical properties.
measurements: Surface and cross-sectional oxide morphology via SEM
Room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated specimens show no significant decrease in oxidation (e.g., similar weight gain or oxide scale failure) compared to uncoated specimens, or if there is a measurable degradation in room- or high-temperature mechanical properties relative to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Structural metallic materials for applications at high temperatures must have a balance of mechanical properties and oxidation resistance. Coated and internally cooled Ni-based superalloys are used in gas turbine engines close to their high temperature limit, which is imposed by the melting temperature of Ni. The search for new alloys with similar or better capabilities at higher temperatures has concentrated on Nb-silicide based alloys that have lower densities, significantly higher solidus temperatures in excess of 1900 °C and can offer notable mechanical properties []. For example, some of these alloys can have compressive yield strength of about 1800 MPa at room temperature, 1200 MPa at 1000 °C and 500 MPa at 1200 °C []. The oxidation resistance of Nb-silicide based alloys was improved dramatically when the key alloying elements Al, Cr, Si, and Ti were in synergy with other transition and refractory metals, for example Hf, Mo, and simple metal and metalloid elements, e.g., Sn [,,,,]. In the case of Sn, the early research [,] concentrated on alloys where its concentration was low to avoid the formation of the A15-Nb3Sn compound. In 2007, Geng et al [] reported that the addition

The research on the oxidation of Nb-silicide-based alloys would suggest (a) that Ge and/or Sn are needed to suppress pest oxidation, and (b) that, when these alloying additions were present individually or simultaneously in the alloys, the spallation of their scales at high temperatures was not suppressed. It is now well established that Ge or Sn has an effect on macrosegregation and can also reduce the liquidus temperature of the alloy. Alloying with Sn can affect the stability of the Nbss but not the alloying with Ge, which can, however, significantly reduce the cracking of the substrate below the scale/substrate interface []. Unfortunately, from the oxidation research on multicomponent Nb-silicide-based alloys, it is not clear whether it was the synergy of Sn or Ge individually or simultaneously with Al, Cr, Si, and Ti that improved oxidation resistance, or whether the presence of oxygen scavenging Hf with/without transition and refractory metals and with some or all of the aforementioned elements was essential for increasing the oxidation resistance.

There are some researches working on the addition of Al [,], Mo [], Ti [], V [], or Zr [], but few of them focus on the elevated-temperature mechanical performance and the overall effect of the constituent elements. To understand the elemental effect on mechanical properties, equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy is firstly designed as a base alloy by adding the high modulus refractory element Mo to HfNbTaTiZr. Then the subtraction method is used to analyze each elemental effect in the equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr. Thus, in this study, six alloys HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi are investigated and compared on their microstructure. Further, the compressive properties at room temperature and at elevated temperature are investigated. By comparing HfMoNbTaTiZr and HfNbTaTiZr, the influence of the addition of Mo can be understood. Likewise, the influence of the addition of Nb, Ta, Ti, or Zr can be articulated. In addition, promising compositions were found and further improved design is suggested. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solid solution strengthening effect will be discussed.
